<reason>PRO built a coherent credibility/asymmetry case and then did the decisive work in the middle rounds: it turned CON's own soft-landing history into evidence for the motion, and its pressure questions forced CON to (a) concede that "patience" meant raising rates substantially and only pausing near the end, and (b) hold both "workers couldn't force catch-up" and "wages catch up later." CON's A1/A2 were honest and labeled, and "catch-up by attrition is not a spiral" is a plausible answer, but the concession narrowed the dispute to the last point of inflation, which PRO exploited to show CON's "brutal" framing (millions idled) sits awkwardly with the motion's stipulated modest rise. CON's distributional/scarring argument stayed live and its closing distinction was clear, but CON never really neutralized PRO's point that persistent above-target inflation with no catch-up is itself a regressive hit on the same workers. PRO's clipped closing was a small execution cost, and CON's fiscal-cushion-is-fiction point landed partly, keeping this competitive rather than decisive.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>PRO's Q2 and follow-up in Rebuttal 2 (A4.3–A4.5): exposing the tension between CON's "workers could not force catch-up raises" and "inflation lets wages catch up later," then arguing either branch damages CON — silent wage cut on the weak, or a de facto second round. CON's "both can be true" reply was reasonable but left CON's policy looking very close to the motion.</best_rebuttal>
